transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

In long meetings, people talk directly to me and I just zone out—I realize afterward I didn’t really hear what they were saying. It’s become a major issue over the last two years since a company restructuring put me into a role with constant back-to-back meetings, and I'm starting to feel really embarrassed and worried about it.
Did you have similar problems with attention, forgetfulness, or being easily distracted when you were a child or in school, before these work meetings started?

Yes, even back in elementary school, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was constantly out of my seat and talking over classmates. I actually got sent to the hallway quite a bit because I couldn't sit still or wait my turn, even though I was smart and did well on tests.
Did these attention and restlessness problems continue through your teens and adulthood, or did they mostly go away until the recent work change?

They never truly went away, but they were much easier to manage when I could stay active and organize my work around my own rhythms. I managed to cope through my teens and earlier career, but the recent restructuring and all these long, sitting meetings have really brought these lifelong struggles to a head.

When you were younger and even now, do you still often act before thinking—for example interrupting people, blurting out answers, or having trouble waiting your turn—more than just feeling inattentive or restless?

Yes, absolutely. Even back in elementary school, my report cards always mentioned me talking over classmates and not being able to wait my turn. Today, I still struggle with it constantly—I'll blurt out answers in meetings before people even finish their questions, or jump into coworkers' conversations and finish their sentences for them without thinking.
Do these impulsive or hyperactive behaviors cause problems in more than one setting, such as at work and at home or in social situations?

Yes, they definitely affect both areas. At work, my restlessness and zoning out lead to embarrassing mistakes in negotiations and force me to work late to fix errors. At home, it's starting to strain my relationship because I'm too distracted and restless to just sit and relax with my partner in the evenings.
Do you also have a long history of being physically very restless and impulsive, like fidgeting, leaving your seat, interrupting, or acting before thinking, not just trouble paying attention?

Yes, I have a long history of that—I'm constantly fidgeting, jiggling my leg, and I often have to get up during meetings because sitting still gives me a wired, crawling feeling inside. I also tend to blurt out answers and interrupt people, which has been a struggle since elementary school when teachers always complained about me being out of my seat and talking over others.
Do you feel that your main problem is being physically restless and impulsive, or is it mostly trouble paying attention and staying organized without much hyperactivity?

I actually experience a combination of both, but the physical restlessness and impulsivity are extremely prominent and hard to control. If I have to sit still, I get a wired, crawling feeling inside that forces me to fidget, pace, or impulsively blurt things out and interrupt others. While I definitely zone out and miss details, that physical urge to always be in motion is a massive, unavoidable part of my daily struggle.

Before age 12, were your main problems mostly being unable to pay attention, or were they equally marked by being very physically restless and impulsive, like constantly fidgeting, leaving your seat, and interrupting others?

Before age 12, my struggles were very much dominated by physical restlessness and impulsivity. My elementary report cards always complained about me being unable to sit still, constantly getting out of my seat, and talking over classmates instead of waiting my turn. I even got sent out into the hallway quite a bit because of it, even though I was smart and did well on tests.
Have you ever had periods of unusually high energy or decreased need for sleep that lasted several days, or is the restlessness something you've had since childhood without those episodes?

No, I have never had distinct periods of unusually high energy or a decreased need for sleep that lasted for days. Instead, this restlessness is a constant, lifelong pattern that dates back to my childhood. Even in elementary school, my teachers wrote on my report cards that I couldn't sit still, was constantly out of my seat, and talked over my classmates.

More history is needed to determine whether this is longstanding and pervasive versus situational and stress-driven.

opening_question.question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Lifelong pattern beginning before age 12 with prominent hyperactivity/impulsivity (constant fidgeting, leaving seat, pacing, interrupting, blurting out, difficulty waiting turn) and inattention (zoning out, missing details), present in more than one setting and causing clear work and relationship impairment. The presentation is best captured as hyperkinetic disorder with combined symptoms rather than inattentive-only ADHD. No evidence for episodic mania.
